svg.title: Monotonic Stack and Monotonic Deque: Next Greater Element and Sliding Window Maximum
svg.desc: Animated step-by-step trace of a monotonic decreasing stack solving Next Greater Element in amortized O(n) time, paired with a monotonic deque maintaining Sliding Window Maximum (k=3) by storing indices, expiring out-of-window front indices, and popping dominated back elements.
svg.text: Monotonic Stack & Monotonic Deque: Amortized O(n) Order Maintenance
Decreasing Stack for Next Greater Element (1 push + at most 1 pop per item) vs Index-Backed Deque for Window Max
Input A = [ 2, 5, 3, 7, 4, 8 ] (pop smaller stack tops when A[i] arrives):
Also computes Largest Rectangle in Histogram
Even though an inner while-loop can pop k elements in a single step:
1. Each index is pushed onto the stack AT MOST ONCE (n total pushes).
2. Once popped, an index never re-enters (at most n total pops).
Total stack ops <= 2n => strictly Theta(n) worst-case time!
Deque State (FRONT = Window Max | BACK = Newest Candidates):

g.text: Outputs = [ ] (index 0 can never be max again)
i=4 (val 5): EXPIRE front 1, POP back 3 & 2, push 4!

svg.text: Rule 1 (Front Expiration): if (deque.front <= i - k) deque.popFront();
Why the Deque Stores Indices (Not Values)
1. O(1) Value Lookup: A[idx] retrieves the value for monotonic back comparisons.
2. O(1) Expiration Check: idx <= i - k detects when the front exits the window.
3. Duplicate Safety: values alone cannot distinguish two equal elements at
different positions inside vs outside [i - k + 1, i].
Both structures achieve strictly O(n) time and O(n) (or O(k) for deque) space because every element enters and exits at most once.
